world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Tawallammat Tamajaq is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's single title-hit, Aikhenvald & Nientao 1988 'On accent in Tamasheq' (3 pp., Russian, Institute of Oriental Studies postgraduate proceedings), is real: confirmed from Maho's EBALL entry 5765 in the Glottolog bibliography and from Aikhenvald's own November 2025 CV (p. 24), but no digital copy exists anywhere reachable and the variety is unspecified (linked by Maho to all four Tuareg languages); priority low. The best first-hand statement actually read is the 'Note sur l'accent touareg' in Prasse, Alojaly & Mohamed 2003 (pp. XX-XXII, held by the project), which covers tawallammat explicitly: weak dynamic accent with high tone, non-contrastive, penultimate on most singular nouns and possessive groups, antepenultimate on suffixed plurals and simple verb tenses, final on closed lists, fixed accent in intensive tenses. second-hand, quotes Prasse, agrees). Still unobtainable: Nicolai 1981 GLECS (tawellemmet-specific, priority high, print only), Louali & Philippson 2005 (Brill, CAPTCHA-walled, priority medium).

new_statements.quote: 1) L'accent touareg est un accent dynamique faible et accompagné d'un ton haut, 2) La place de l'accent varie selon la structure de la phrase (l'accent n'a donc pas de rôle distinctif; il n'existe pas de paires minimales de mots distingués par la place de l'accent, sauf par accident absolu), 3) Les groupes enclitiques jouent un grand rôle [...] Accent sur la pénultième. La majorité des noms singuliers [...] Accent sur l'antépénultième. Les pluriels à désinence. Les pl.1 gardent donc l'accent sur la même syllabe que le singulier. [...] On peut dire que les deux temps simples des verbes ont un accent antépénultième latent
new_statements.translation: 1) The Tuareg accent is a weak dynamic accent accompanied by a high tone, 2) The position of the accent varies according to the structure of the phrase (the accent therefore has no distinctive role; there are no minimal pairs of words distinguished by the position of the accent, except by pure accident), 3) Enclitic groups play a large role [...] Accent on the penult: the majority of singular nouns [...] Accent on the antepenult: plurals with a suffix. The pl.1 thus keep the accent on the same syllable as the singular. [...] One may say that the two simple tenses of the verb have a latent antepenultimate accent.
new_statements.citation: Prasse, Karl-G., Ghoubeïd Alojaly & Ghabdouane Mohamed. 2003. Dictionnaire touareg-français (Niger), Tome I: A-L. Copenhagen: Museum Tusculanum Press.
new_statements.locator: Introduction, 'Note sur l'accent touareg', pp. XX-XXII (PDF pp. 19-21 of the saved text PDF; quoted sentences on p. XX, verb rule on p. XXI)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (542 pp., archive.org upload, text layer) and its the scanned text), and rendered PDF pp. 19-21 to PNG (80 dpi) and read the page images. Printed folios at the foot of the pages are XX, XXI, XXII (the scanned misreads XXII as 'XXI'; the image is unambiguous), so the locator 'pp. XX-XXII = PDF pp. 19-21' is correct. Every quoted sentence is on the page as quoted: p. XX 'Note sur l'accent touareg.. 1) L'accent touareg est un accent dynamique faible et accompagné d'un ton haut, 2) La place de l'accent varie selon la structure de la phrase (l'accent n'a donc pas de rôle distinctif; il n'existe pas de paires minimales de mots distingués par la place de l'accent, sauf par accident absolu),…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive pitch accent-like stress (weak dynamic, high tone) whose position is set by morphological class and by the enclitic group rather than by a single positional rule: singular nouns (and Arabic -at loans, internal plurals, most polysyllabic pronouns) carry it on the penult; suffixed plurals keep it on the same stem syllable as the singular (so antepenult), as do vowel-final singulars, deverbal nouns, verbal adjectives and the simple (aorist/perfect) verb tenses, whose 'latent antepenultimate' accent moves onto a preceding particle or conjunction when one is available; final accent is limited to closed exceptional classes; the intensive perfect and imperfect have a fixed accent on a theme syllable regardless of phrase structure. Adding a possessive or object clitic shifts the accent toward the end of the enclitic group so that it stays penultimate in the group.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned: plural+possessive groups like iɣătemăn-in 'avec un accent secondaire antérieur'; in intensive tenses 'Quand la syllabe accentuée est antérieure à l'antépénultième, cette dernière reçoit pourtant un accent secondaire' (p. XXII).
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in 'espèces exceptionnelles': kalá 'non', wală 'rien', kullú 'tout', numerals 2-10, certain deictic suffixes (-en, -nad, -nin, -di), many disyllabic interjections, French loans (fărtí, kăntí, otél), and in Tawallammat plurals that lost a final -a (tifír for tifira). Intensive tenses have a fixed morphological accent. Weak verbs ending in a vowel keep the accent as if the lost syllable were present. In Tawallammat the diphthongization of final -e/-o to -ăy/-ăw does not move the accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Accent is stated to vary with phrase structure; rules are given for isolated (citation) words and for enclitic groups (noun+possessive, preposition+pronoun, particle+verb, verb+object clitic). The dictionary marks accent only on intensive perfects (circumflex/acute).
new_statements.identity_note: Prasse, Alojaly & Mohamed 2003 is explicitly bi-dialectal: 'la tawallammat de l'est (dial. de l'Azawagh, sigle W)' based on the Kel-Eghlal speech = Tawallammat tan Dannag, tawa1286, and 'la tayart (dial. de l'Ayr, sigle Y)' based on Kel-Ferwan = Air Tamajeq tayr1257 (thz). The accent note is written for both, with specific Tawallammat remarks (diphthongised finals, plurals that lost -a). The supporting Prasse 1972 Manuel describes Tahaggart (taha1241) with first-hand footnotes on WE (Kel-Dennek/Kel-Eghlal Tawallammat). Sudlow 2011, filed under tawa1286 by Glottolog, describes the Tamaghit/Tudalt dialects of Oudalan, Burkina Faso, and is silent on stress placement.

new_statements.translation: 1) The Tuareg accent is a weak dynamic accent accompanied by a high tone, 2) The position of the accent varies with the structure of the phrase (so the accent has no distinctive role; there are no minimal pairs of words distinguished by accent position, except by pure accident) [...] Accent on the penultimate: the majority of singular nouns [...] Accent on the antepenultimate: plurals with a suffix [...] The simple tenses of verbs [...] have a latent antepenultimate accent [...] In Tawallammat the diphthongization of -e, -o has no influence on the position of the accent
new_statements.citation: Prasse, Karl-G., Ghoubeid Alojaly & Ghabdouane Mohamed. 2003. Dictionnaire touareg-français (Niger), Tome I: A-L. Copenhagen: Museum Tusculanum Press. Introduction, 'Note sur l'accent touareg', pp. XX-XXII.
new_statements.locator: pp. XX-XXII ('Note sur l'accent touareg'); the tawallammat-specific sentence is on p. XXI
new_statements.reading: First-hand description by Prasse with two native co-authors, explicitly covering tawallammat (eastern, Azawagh) alongside tayart. Word accent is non-contrastive and morphologically/syntactically determined: penultimate in most singular nouns, internal plurals and noun + possessive-enclitic groups (the accent moves rightward to stay penultimate); antepenultimate in suffixed plurals, vowel-final singulars and the simple verb tenses (latent antepenultimate, migrating onto a preceding proclitic); final only in closed classes (numerals, some deictics, French loans, tawallammat plurals that lost -a); intensive tenses have fixed morphological accent. For a word-stress catalog this is a mixed penultimate/antepenultimate, morphology-driven, non-lexical system with a pitch (high-tone) correlate.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

new_statements.quote: In the stative aspect of the verb, a vowel can be heavily stressed. It is longer than a standard long vowel and heavily accented. These are written: â, î, ê, û, ô (even ǝ̂ although this is rare). [p. 24] ... The stative differs from the perfective only by the one vowel (or by the stress placed on one vowel). When this vowel is highly stressed the stative is easy to recognise but, in conversational Tamasheq, the amount of stress put on the vowel will vary depending on what the speaker is or isn't emphasising. It can then be difficult to distinguish between a perfective and a stative that is not heavily stressed (although their meanings are so close this hardly matters). [p. 84]
new_statements.citation: Sudlow, David (2001). The Tamasheq of North-East Burkina Faso. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. 358 pp.
new_statements.locator: Sect. 3.1 Pronunciation, p. 24 (PDF p. 34); sect. 3.20 Uses of the stative, p. 84 (PDF p. 94); cf. 'Syntax and stress', p. 43 (PDF p. 53), which concerns emphasis by word order, and p. 7 ('natural rhythm and stress')
new_statements.relation_note: Silent on placement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's penult/antepenult morphological accent (Prasse et al. 2003). Its one statement — a heavily stressed, over-long vowel as the mark of the stative/intensive perfect, with its salience depending on emphasis — is compatible with Prasse's note that the intensive tenses carry a fixed morphological accent, and with the non-distinctive status of accent (the stative contrast rides on vowel length plus stress, not on stress alone). Caveat on identity: the language described is Oudalan Tamasheq (Tamaghit 'Sa' and Tudalt 'Za'), i.e. Malian-type Tamasheq; Tudalt is 'an offshoot' of the Meneka Western Tawellemmet dialect, which is p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for the position of word stress is given anywhere in the book. The only stress statement is morphological: the stative aspect ('the intensive form of the perfect') is marked by one over-long, heavily stressed vowel (written with a circumflex), and the degree of stress on that vowel varies with the speaker's emphasis, so an unstressed stative can sound like a perfective.
new_statements.exceptions: None on placement. The 'Syntax and stress' heading (p. 43) is about emphasis through word order (SVO/VSO/topicalisation/cleft), not prosodic stress. Appendix 6.2-6.3 on Western (Meneka) and Eastern (Tahoua) Tawellemmet lists pronunciation, grammar and vocabulary differences with no stress remark.
new_statements.identity_note: Sudlow describes the Tamasheq of Oudalan province, NE Burkina Faso: Tamaghit ('sha' dialect, 'very similar to Tadghaq' of Kidal, i.e. Malian Tamasheq taq/tama1365) and Tudalt ('za' dialect, 'an offshoot' of the Meneka Western Tawellemmet dialect). The Tawellemmet of Tahoua, the core of tawa1286, is treated only contrastively in Appendix 6.3 (pronunciation, pronouns, vocabulary), with no stress remark. Sudlow himself says the Tamasheq of Tahoua-Tchin Tabaraden 'is relatively close to Tudalt' and that his data 'most closely applies to the Gossi-Gao-Meneka-Filinge-Niamey-Bankalari-Gorom-Tessit region'. The copy opened is the 2011 second revised edition, not the 2001 first edition listed by Glottolog. Aikhenvald & Nientao 1988 is coded by Maho for four Tuareg languages (thv, ttq, taq, thz) and its variety is unknown.

sources.quote: La mise en exergue de l'existence de l'accent en touareg a conduit à conclure que l'accent touareg n'est pas pertinent. [...] PRASSE & al. (2003) précise qu'il existe plusieurs cas dans lesquels l'accent est mis sur la pénultième syllabe : « La majorité des noms singuliers ədékəl "paume de la main", akắtab "écriture", eɣắzar "mare") et les noms avec une forme féminine en –t (teɣǎtemt "chaussure", tǎzzắgrǎt "hauteur, longueur") suivent cette règle. [...] En présence d'un pronom possessif, l'accent se déplace vers la fin du groupe enclitique et l'accent reste sur la pénultième : ifukan-nắsǎn, akắtáb-in, eɣatém-net.
sources.locator: Sect. 0.12.6 'Prosodie du touareg' and 0.12.7 'Accent en touareg', pp. 41-42
sources.note: Second-hand: a tawəlləmmət/tayərt-focused thesis that quotes Chaker 1989 (no phonological intensity accent in Berber), Prasse 1959/1972 (three accent grades; no minimal pairs) and Prasse et al. 2003 (penultimate on most singular nouns, enclitic shift, polysyllabic pronouns), and concludes accent is not phonologically pertinent and matters only diachronically/comparatively. Endorses, does not contradict, Prasse's description for these two Niger dialects.
